clue.text: Withdraw from diocese, pocketing church key

indicators.note: to pocket something is to take it inside, so one word goes into another

blocks.note: a see is a bishop's diocese
CE is the Church of England
D is a musical key

explanation.surface: A cleric quits the diocese, taking the church key away in a pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: The church and the key go into the diocese together, side by side, rather than one at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: To secede is to formally leave a union, federation or organisation, a kind of withdrawal.

clue.text: Guarded point made by Peter tappin' the keys

blocks.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
tapping keys is typing, with the dropped G as in the clue

explanation.surface: A sharp point produced by a man called Peter tapping at a keyboard.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter looks like a typist's name; it is safecracker's slang. The apostrophe in tappin' tells you to drop the final G.
explanation.definitionFit: A safety pin has its sharp tip covered by a clasp, so its point is shielded.

clue.text: Move nearer for photograph

blocks.note: first meaning: to draw together, narrowing a gap
second meaning: a picture taken at very short range

explanation.surface: A photographer asking the subjects to squeeze in for the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Ranks close up when they draw together, and a picture shot from very short range has the same name.

clue.text: One capped while still at school

definitions.text: One capped while still at school

blocks.clueFragment: One capped while still at school
blocks.note: surface reading: a pupil chosen to play for the national team, which in Britain earns a cap
setter's reading: the slow pupil made to wear a conical paper hat as punishment

explanation.walkthrough: In British sport, being capped means being picked for the national side; the cap here is the pointed paper hat once put on a poor pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow-witted pupil was traditionally made to wear a pointed paper hat in class as a humiliation.

clue.text: Does he need to get pardon over taking in wife?

definitions.text: Does he need to get pardon over taking in wife?

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside, so one piece sits within another
in a horizontal answer, turning a word over flips it to read the other way round

blocks.note: taken as written
W is the standard abbreviation for wife
to remit a sin or penalty is to pardon it

explanation.surface: A rhetorical question about a husband who has to beg forgiveness from his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: TO takes in W to make TWO, then REMIT reversed gives TIMER. The whole clue doubles as the definition: an unfaithful man is the one who needs pardon from his wife.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-timer is a deceiver, especially a partner who cheats, so he is the man who would beg forgiveness.

clue.text: It may cause agitation about the family's dirty linen

definitions.text: It may cause agitation about the family's dirty linen

blocks.clueFragment: agitation about the family's dirty linen
blocks.note: surface reading: distress over a household's private scandals, as in washing dirty linen in public
setter's reading: the literal churning of soiled sheets and clothes in a drum

explanation.walkthrough: Dirty linen is an idiom for private scandal; read literally, it is laundry being churned about.
explanation.definitionFit: A domestic laundry appliance cleans clothes by agitating them in soapy water in a rotating drum.

clue.text: Viscount was such a high-flyer, but with poor PR came to grief

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the type of aircraft

indicators.note: something that came to grief has been wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A nobleman who rose high but was brought down by bad publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: The Viscount looks like an aristocrat but is the Vickers Viscount, a 1950s British airliner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vickers Viscount airliner was powered by propellers driven by gas turbines, the engine type the answer names.

clue.text: Man, perhaps, taken in by crazy fool

indicators.note: being taken in by something means being held inside it

blocks.note: mad means crazy
the Isle of Man is one example

explanation.surface: A man duped by a mad idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man, perhaps' is the Isle of Man, the island in the Irish Sea; 'perhaps' shows it is one example of the word wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: To fool someone is to deceive them, giving a false impression, which is what misleading means.

clue.text: Ring-leader small boy turned on

indicators.note: the leader is the one at the front, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of this word
a boy's name, short for Andrew

explanation.surface: A gang's ringleader turns on a little boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' reads as attacked, but it means aroused. Randy is British slang for sexually eager.
explanation.definitionFit: Randy is informal for lustful or sexually excited, the state of someone aroused.

clue.text: Outstanding leader with the customary native servant

blocks.note: standard means usual or customary
in British India a bearer was a household servant

explanation.surface: A great chief accompanied by his usual local servant, a scene from the Raj.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise but here means prominent; the flag carrier is literally at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard-bearer carries a flag at the head of troops, and figuratively leads a movement or cause.

clue.text: Author's understatements?

blocks.note: surface reading: a writer's habit of playing things down
setter's reading: statements placed literally under the main text, at the bottom of the page

explanation.walkthrough: Understatement normally means modesty of expression; here it is split into 'under' and 'statements', the remarks printed beneath the text.
explanation.definitionFit: Footnotes are remarks an author prints at the bottom of a page, literally below the main text.

clue.text: Fall again bringing product from trees

blocks.note: RE is a prefix meaning again
to fall, as from grace, is to sin

explanation.surface: Something tumbling a second time and producing a tree product.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives 'Fall' first, but 'again' supplies the front of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Resin is the sticky substance exuded by pines and other trees, used in varnish and amber.

clue.text: Across the border the outsiders exercise

indicators.note: outsiders are those on the edge, so only the first and last letters are kept
one thing lying across another straddles it, so it goes round the middle piece

blocks.note: the two edge letters of this word
a hem is the border of a garment

explanation.surface: Instructions for a workout that crosses a frontier with outsiders.
explanation.walkthrough: The outer letters T and E sit either side of HEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is a short essay set as a school exercise, a sense common in older British usage.

clue.text: Oil moneys misused in an offensive way

indicators.note: something misused is put to the wrong purpose, so the letters are rearranged wrongly

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Petrodollars spent in a distasteful, objectionable manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means foul or objectionable, so the adverb describes doing something in an offensive manner.

clue.text: Tradesman bound to go to the wall

definitions.text: Tradesman bound to go to the wall

blocks.clueFragment: bound to go to the wall
blocks.note: surface reading: a businessman certain to fail, since going to the wall means going bankrupt
setter's reading: a decorator whose job literally takes him to the wall

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go to the wall' is an idiom for business failure; the decorator who sticks up wallpaper does it literally every day.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper-hanger is a decorator who pastes wallpaper onto walls, a skilled tradesman.

clue.text: Dissolute artist — type Hades swallowed up?

indicators.note: something swallowed is held inside whatever ate it

blocks.note: RA is a Royal Academician
to type is to key, as on a keyboard
Hades is the underworld

explanation.surface: Asking whether a debauched painter is the sort Hades devours.
explanation.walkthrough: The underworld goes inside the typing word just before its last letter, not in its exact middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Rakehelly is an archaic adjective meaning like a rakehell, a wildly immoral, debauched man.

clue.text: Boxer, perhaps, that has no chance?

blocks.note: first meaning: a boxer is a breed of this animal
second meaning: in racing slang, a hopeless runner or loser

explanation.surface: Asking whether a prizefighter is a hopeless case.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxer looks like a fighter, but it is the breed; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer is one breed of pet canine, and slang uses the same word for a hopeless loser or no-hoper.

clue.text: Lodger has damaged fuel storage tank

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so the letters are put in another order

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A tenant has wrecked the tank where fuel is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A gasholder, or gasometer, is the large telescoping tank in which town gas is stored.

clue.text: Head teachers

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for the head
second meaning: the National Union of Teachers, a British trade union

explanation.walkthrough: 'Head teachers' reads as school principals; split, it is two separate meanings. The NUT was the main teachers' union in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Nut is informal slang for a person's skull, and the initials of a British teaching union spell it too.

clue.text: Soldiers execute captured enemy leader, and feel sick

indicators.note: a captive is held inside, so one piece goes within another
the leader goes first, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's reserve force
to execute is to kill
the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Troops shoot a captured enemy commander and are left feeling queasy.
explanation.walkthrough: The enemy's first letter goes into the execute word just after its opening letter; the Territorial Army is Britain's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: To take ill is an idiom for falling sick, becoming unwell, which matches feeling sick.

clue.text: Teases about not being alert to serious crimes

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word surrounds the second

blocks.note: to kid is to tease
someone napping is dozing, caught off guard

explanation.surface: Mocking someone for failing to notice grave offences.
explanation.definitionFit: Kidnapping is the abduction of a person, usually for ransom, among the gravest offences in law.

clue.text: Compose uplifting melody as part of suite

indicators.note: in a down answer, lifting a word up makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to pen is to write or compose
a tune is a melody

explanation.surface: Writing an inspiring tune for a movement of an orchestral suite.
explanation.walkthrough: The suite is Holst's The Planets, whose movements are each named after a planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Holst's orchestral suite The Planets has seven movements, the last named after the god-planet of the sea.

clue.text: She bakes with hot ingredients, making a bit of money

indicators.note: ingredients are mixed together in baking, so the letters are blended into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A woman who earns some cash by baking with hot ingredients.
explanation.definitionFit: Baksheesh is a small tip or gratuity, from Persian, especially one given in the Middle East.

clue.text: It's pointless to be so outspoken

blocks.note: first meaning: without a sharp point or edge
second meaning: frank and direct in speech

explanation.surface: Someone says there is no use being so frank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointless' reads as futile; literally, it means lacking a point.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull knife lacks an edge or tip, and a person who speaks frankly without tact is described the same way.

clue.text: Animal — with it, river may be connected

blocks.note: hip means fashionable, with it
the Po is Italy's longest river

explanation.surface: A creature associated with a river, which it may well be connected to.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the beast is short for hippopotamus, Greek for river horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The hippo is a large African mammal that lives in and around rivers and lakes.

clue.text: Bird carried by another one

indicators.note: what is carried is held within, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: One bird being carried on the back of another.
explanation.definitionFit: The heron is a long-legged wading bird with a dagger bill, found by rivers and marshes.

clue.text: Unmarried woman, an angel

indicators.note: read as un-married, it says take away the abbreviation for married

blocks.note: a woman's name
M is the abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: A single woman described as a real angel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unmarried' looks like a description of the woman; it is the instruction to drop M from MURIEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Uriel is one of the archangels named in Jewish and Christian tradition and in Milton's Paradise Lost.

clue.text: Evasive action to control part of fight

blocks.note: to run a business is to control it
a round is one part of a boxing bout

explanation.surface: A boxer dodging to take charge of one stage of the bout.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving someone the run-around means evading them with excuses and deceptive delays.

clue.text: Cart backing on slope into combat area

indicators.note: a vehicle backing goes in reverse, so the word is read from end to start

blocks.note: a tilt is a slope or slant
a dray is a low cart for heavy loads such as beer barrels

explanation.surface: A cart reversing down a slope into a battle zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' places the turned-round cart after the slope in this across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiltyard was an enclosed ground where medieval knights jousted, a tilt being a joust.

clue.text: Make beloved mine at last in Arden in disguise

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of the word before it
a disguise changes appearance, so the letters are rearranged to look different

blocks.note: the final letter of this word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean scene: winning affection in the Forest of Arden while in disguise, as Rosalind does.
explanation.definitionFit: To endear is to cause someone to be loved or liked, making them dear to others.
